title: EU enlargement reform: Challenges and debates

## Briefing

##### EPRS |  European Parliamentary Research Service

## EU enlargement reform: Challenges and debates

Jakub Przetacznik and Silvia Kotanidis with Laura Zghibarta, Members' Research Service Published: October 2026 | Document number: PE 796.998

#### In this briefing

• Background 
• European Commission proposals 
• Member States' positions 
• Do the EU Treaties allow special or partial membership? 
• Accession negotiations: Latest developments 
• Candidate countries' reactions to enlargement reform proposals 
• European Parliament positions 
• Expert proposals for enlargement reform 

### Summary

The European Union (EU) last enlarged in 2013 when Croatia joined. Since then, several countries in the EU's southern and eastern neighbourhoods have been granted candidate status and have been progressing on their accession path. The EU has sought to advance its enlargement agenda in a way that upholds its values and standards, reflects its capacity to accommodate new members, secures Member States' consensus and responds to geopolitical pressures. Reconciling these objectives is the central challenge of enlargement reform. The European Commission was exploring a 'reverse enlargement' approach in 2025. This model reverses the usual sequence and reshuffles the accession order: formal EU membership, with limited rights and obligations, would precede completion of reforms and access to full membership benefits. Following their rejection of this proposal, Member States have stepped up their contributions to the debate on redesigning the enlargement and accession model. Proposals from Germany and France envisage greater benefits alongside progress on reforms, with full membership following later. The Commission's latest proposal similarly focuses on strengthening gradual integration. While the Commission and national capitals discuss the revised approach, preparations for enlargement are proceeding on several fronts: pre‑accession arrangements, treaty‑based post‑accession arrangements, and internal EU reforms to prepare for a Union of more than 30 Member

States. Drawing on the need for reform, the urgency of enlargement and candidate countries' varying progress towards accession, experts and analysts have contributed their own proposals to the debate.

### Background

Ursula von der Leyen described the European Commission she led during her first term as president 
(2019‑2024) as a 'geopolitical Commission', aiming to advance enlargement and stabilise the EU's 
neighbourhood. There was a recognised need to give momentum to enlargement, restore the 
credibility of the prospect of EU membership for the Western Balkans and push against competing 
influences from third countries, in particular Russia (e.g. information operations, political and economic 
influence) and China (e.g. investments and economic presence). Against this background, the 
Commission introduced a revised enlargement methodology in 2020. Based on four principles: 
credibility, predictability, dynamism and stronger political steering, it introduced thematic clusters 
based negotiations to speed up the process. 
Russia's full‑scale war of aggression against Ukraine that began in 2022 made enlargement policy 
even more important strategically. Having had already extensive political and economic relations 
with the EU through bilateral association agreements but fuelled by security concerns, Ukraine, 
Moldova and Georgia immediately requested to join the EU, with the former two currently negotiating. 
The Commission recognised this as a historic moment in bilateral relations, grounded in legitimate 
aspirations of the countries to join the Union.

Currently, the enlargement process and accession negotiations face a range of challenges. They relate 
to the EU's decision‑making, e.g. the 'proliferation of decision points' requiring unanimity, and bilateral 
issues between Member States and candidate countries. Challenges are also tied to concerns about 
the costs of enlargement and the risk of post‑accession backsliding. Moreover, there are requirements 
for internal EU reforms to ensure that an enlarged Union functions, but no consensus on what these 
reforms should entail. 
At the EU level, the enlargement methodology has also come under scrutiny, with calls for adaptation. 
The calmer political and security context underpinning the 2020 methodological reform is seen 
as ill‑suited to the post-2022 geopolitical environment. Stagnation in the enlargement process is 
considered to have created a vacuum that can be readily exploited by Russia and China through 
interference and other forms of influence (e.g. hybrid threats, election interference, foreign information 
manipulation and interference operations, projects that create economic dependencies, and security 
cooperation). This creates external geopolitical pressure for the EU to act more rapidly and decisively 
on enlargement. While remaining a merit‑based process, enlargement is regarded as 'a strategic 
investment in Europe's security and stability', with failure to pursue it carrying greater risks and costs 
for Europe. 

### European Commission proposals

The revised enlargement methodology of 2020 also envisaged that sufficient progress on reform 
priorities agreed during negotiations should lead to closer integration, as well as 'accelerated 
integration and "phasing‑in" to individual EU policies, the EU market and EU programmes'. This became 
an official framework for enlargement policy and was subsequently endorsed in the June 2022 
European Council conclusions, which invited the EU institutions 'to further advance the gradual 
integration between the European Union and the region already during the enlargement process itself 
in a reversible and merit‑based manner'. 
The Commission's 2025 enlargement report specified that 'accelerated, or gradual, integration seeks to 
bring some of the benefits of future EU accession into the pre‑accession stage by allowing a candidate 
country to integrate into specific areas of EU policy, notably parts of the EU single market, once 
legislative alignment and the capacity to implement the EU acquis [in the given area] is in place'. This 
approach is intended to incentivise early implementation of the EU acquis and make the transition to 
full membership smoother. 
In 2025, the Commission initiated discussions about a modified enlargement process to better 
support Ukraine and overcome the enlargement deadlock. One notable proposal was dubbed 'reverse 
enlargement' or phased integration, and envisaged partial accession. Candidate countries would 
formally join the EU with limited rights and obligations and observer‑like functions. They would 
subsequently complete the required reforms (e.g. in the areas of anti‑corruption and the rule of law), 
fully adopt the EU acquis and acquire full membership rights. This format would have prioritised 
Ukraine and possibly be extended to other candidate countries. 
An alternative option was to maintain the status quo, leaving the enlargement policy unchanged, with 
frontrunners Montenegro and Albania potentially joining before the end of 2029. 
Another pathway entailed the deepening of 'gradual integration' by allowing candidate countries to 
participate in more EU programmes before formal accession. This option was taken forward by the 
Commission in its communication entitled 'Preparing for a wider Union' (see the Section on 'Accession 
negotiations: Latest developments'). 
The Commission has also laid out general principles guiding its approach to enlargement reform. Marta 
Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, has stressed that no shortcuts on reforms would 
be allowed, and that strong safeguards against backsliding should be embedded in future accession 
treaties without creating a two‑tier membership system for countries that have aligned with the EU 
acquis. The importance of EU reforms to accommodate more than 30 Member States has also been 
emphasised. At the structured dialogue with the European Parliament in April 2026, Commissioner 
Kos reiterated and expanded these principles and the central role of fundamentals, highlighting direct 
benefits for citizens and businesses under gradual integration. 

### Member States' positions

Member States have rejected the idea of 'reverse enlargement', citing demanding accession requirements, including their own domestic legal requirements, and concerns that new members could backslide democratically and obstruct the EU agenda. Legal challenges might also concern the legality,

under the Treaties, of limited or partial membership (see the Section on 'Do the EU Treaties allow 
special or partial membership?'). 
Candidate countries are also required to meet the Copenhagen criteria, which complement the 
accession conditions and EU values set out in Articles 49 and 2 of the Treaty on European Union (TEU) 
respectively. These criteria are reflected in the negotiating frameworks and remain central to Member 
States' positions. 
Finally, the reservations of some Member States could complicate the ratification of accession treaties, 
one of the final steps in the accession process, since Article 49 requires ratification by all Member 
States and the applicant country in accordance with their respective constitutional requirements. 
Additionally, Germany has voiced objections to Ukraine's target accession date of 2027, while Austria, 
Sweden and France have reportedly emphasised the primacy of conditionality over speed. 
In response to Commissioner Kos' request to Member States to participate in reforming the 
enlargement process, several proposals have emerged. Germany's and France's proposals for Ukraine 
centre on pre‑accession benefits and status. The German model of 'associate membership' envisages 
substantial representation in EU institutions. Ukraine would participate in meetings of the European 
Council and the Council of the EU and would have associate members of the Commission and the 
European Parliament with no voting rights, as well as an Associate Judge (an Assistant Rapporteur) 
at the European Court of Justice. The proposal includes progressive application of the EU acquis and 
step‑by‑step access to EU programmes under direct management (but not to the entire EU budget). 
To prevent backsliding, it proposes a snap‑back mechanism or, alternatively, a sunset clause. It also 
envisages an important security guarantee for Ukraine: a political commitment by the Member States 
to apply Article 42(7) TEU to Ukraine. 
This proposed status differs from the status of associated country, which, in the case of Ukraine, 
stems from its association agreement with the EU signed in 2014, which contains more limited political 
provisions and provisions on cooperation, and establishes a Deep and Comprehensive Free Trade Area. 
The French proposal for an 'integrated state status' would accelerate Ukraine's accession, though it 
would exclude it from receiving funding under the common agricultural policy (CAP) and cohesion 
policy until full membership is granted. These statuses, conferred through a political declaration, would 
carry strong symbolic value, extend the EU's mutual assistance clause to Ukraine, heighten the visibility 
of progress and offer greater access to other funding programmes, as advancements in reforms and 
negotiations advance. 
In preparation for the EU‑Western Balkans Summit and the EU‑Moldova Summit in June 2026, France 
and Germany co-developed a non-paper entitled 'A New Momentum for Enlargement' covering the 
Western Balkans and Moldova. The proposal centres on streamlining a merit‑ and incentives‑based 
accession process focused more on reforms than procedure and is linked to a pre‑accession strategy
